source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC4453639 (Br J Cancer 112(3):580-593), read in full in my own browser tab: all running text, Tables 1-4 (HTML), and Figures 1, 2 and 3a-3b on the PMC figure pages (images enlarged in the tab to read every value). Online Supplementary Materials S1-S5 (search terms, confounders, sensitivity results, study lists, study-level estimates) not read.

claims.overstatement: Mostly careful (association wording, no absolute risks, biases named). Three points. (1) Study counts: '(52 studies)' and '(54 studies)' attached to the light-drinking estimates are the totals of studies for each site at any intake; Table 2 shows the light-drinking estimates rest on 26 studies (4 cohort + 22 case-control) for the mouth and pharynx and 34 (10 + 24) for oesophageal SCC. The breast count (115, editors' count) is right and is computed the same way from Table 2, so the claim mixes two kinds of count. (2) 'Statistically clear only in Asian studies' is true of the split by area, which is how the paper puts it, but the light-drinking excess was also statistically clear in men (1.20 and 1.39, Table 3) and in case-control studies (1.22 and 1.29, Table 2), and the differences between areas were not significant (P = 0.375 and 0.503). As worded it overstates the regional contrast. (3) The confounding and reference-group caveats omit the authors' sensitivity analyses: keeping only adjusted estimates, and dropping studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, did not materially change results (figures only in Supplementary S3). 'Up to 12.5 g a day on average' paraphrases a category whose midpoint is at most 12.5 g/day: acceptable. No advice on amounts, no 'safe' wording.
claims.note: Every relative risk, interval and I² value from this source checked against Figure 2 (enlarged) and, where given, the Results text: mouth and pharynx 1.13 (1.00-1.26; 26%), oesophageal SCC 1.26 (1.06-1.50; 68%), breast 1.04 (1.01-1.07; 63%), prostate 1.04 (1.01-1.08), colorectum 0.99 (0.95-1.04), liver 1.00 (0.85-1.18), larynx 0.87 (0.68-1.11), lung 0.84 (0.79-0.88), oesophageal AC and gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76-0.98), kidney 0.92 (0.86-0.99), thyroid 0.81 (0.74-0.88), Hodgkin's 0.73 (0.59-0.89), non-Hodgkin's 0.88 (0.80-0.97): all match. Asian subgroup 1.33 (1.06-1.68; 7 studies) and 1.54 (1.18-2.00; 11 studies) match Table 4. Editors' count for breast at light drinking: 42 cohort + 73 case-control = 115 (Table 2): same. 297 of 572 adjusted and 138/572 = 24.1% with occasional drinkers in the reference group: same. 'Former drinkers not separated' is a fair reading: the review records only whether occasional drinkers were in the reference group and lists possible former drinkers among nondrinkers as a limitation. The claim is right that the lower lung and oesophageal adenocarcinoma figures are in Figure 2 and not in the text. The text in fact says the adenocarcinoma was not significantly associated, which contradicts the figure's light estimate. Lung light estimates below 1 also appear in every subgroup row of Tables 2-4. The fitted dose-response curve for lung (Figure 3) rises from RR 1 with no dip at low intake, which supports the claim's point that the low-intake shape is uncertain. The GBD 2016 sentence is not from this source.

Discussion, 2nd paragraph links the Asian finding to the ALDH2 variant carried by 28-45% of people there.

Light drinking: oral cavity and pharynx men 1.20 (1.06-1.35; 12 studies) vs women 1.00 (0.78-1.27; 8); oesophageal SCC men 1.39 (1.11-1.74; 16) vs women 1.14 (0.87-1.49; 8). Outside the split by area, the light-drinking excess was also statistically clear in men, and in case-control studies (Table 2).

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 ('Adjusted estimates' and 'Occasional drinker in reference category' columns)
anchors.extracted: 572 studies (1956-2012; 409 case-control, 163 cohort; 486,538 cases). 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates, and 138 (24.1%) put occasional drinkers with abstainers in the reference category. By site (adjusted / occasional drinkers in reference, of all studies): oral cavity and pharynx 41/20 of 52; oesophageal SCC 32/21 of 54; breast 41/15 of 118; prostate 11/11 of 43; lung 31/8 of 34; kidney 5/5 of 17; thyroid 4/1 of 9.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Intake converted to g/day at 12.5 g per drink (0.8 g/ml, 28 g/ounce). Each reported category is assigned its midpoint (1.2 x the lower bound for an open top category). Light, moderate and heavy drinking = midpoint at most 12.5, at most 50, and above 50 g/day. Whether the nondrinker reference included occasional drinkers was recorded; former drinkers are not handled as a separate group. Adjusted estimates were used when available; otherwise unadjusted RRs were computed from raw data.

Sensitivity analyses limited to adjusted estimates, and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference category, did not materially change results; the figures are only in Supplementary Material S3 (not read). The prostate association was clearer in those analyses.

Limitations the authors state: high heterogeneity for some cancers; drinking patterns and beverage types not examined. Under-reporting of intake by drinkers may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations. Former drinkers may be included among nondrinkers (people with preclinical symptoms stop drinking), which would dilute drinkers' risk. Publication bias is not examined here but referred to the group's earlier single-site meta-analyses.

The authors state that drinking was associated with oral cavity and pharynx, oesophageal SCC and female breast cancer even at low doses. They cite their own 2013 modelled estimate of about 5000 oral and pharyngeal, 24,000 oesophageal SCC and 5000 breast cancer deaths attributable to light drinking worldwide in 2004.

anchors.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3 (fitted dose-response curves, 0-100 g/day)
anchors.extracted: In the continuous meta-regression (fractional polynomials, RR 1 at zero intake), pancreas, lung and prostate show a slight linear increase. The lung curve rises from 1 with no dip at low intake, despite the categorical light RR of 0.84. Oesophageal AC and gastric cardia shows no significant trend. Kidney and thyroid curves fall below 1 at lower doses, lymphoma risk falls linearly, and stomach and liver risk rises from about 25 g/day.

The authors read oesophageal AC and gastric cardia as no association (6th, 11th paragraphs). They attribute the inverse lymphoma association possibly in part to people quitting or cutting down with early symptoms (7th). They read moderate drinking as supporting a protective effect on renal cell cancer (8th), yet the conclusion lists kidney among cancers with no association (11th).

claims.overstatement: Association wording throughout, and causation is explicitly attributed to IARC: no causal overstatement. Minor points. (1) The design contrast picks liver (2.79 vs 1.12) and larynx (2.81 vs 1.12) without saying the design-heterogeneity tests were not significant there (P = 0.226 and 0.216); the only significant design difference was for the mouth and pharynx (P = 0.007), where the claim's own magnitude gives the figures. (2) The point that only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates, so smoking and other differences were often not accounted for, omits that the adjusted-only sensitivity analysis did not materially change results (Supplementary S3, not read). It also omits the authors' specific caveat for lung (no association in never-smokers in their 2011 meta-analysis) and stomach. (3) The colon and rectum association is presented for everyone: the authors found it significantly stronger in men (P = 0.010) and no significant association in women. (4) Melanoma was clear in North American studies and also only in cohort studies (2 studies); the claim gives only the first. (5) 'Oesophageal adenocarcinoma' is the review's 'adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia'. No advice on amounts.
claims.note: Every number from this source matches. 572 studies, 1956-2012, 486,538 cases; 236 (41.3%) North America, 184 (32.2%) Europe, 101 (17.7%) Asia; 138 (24.1%) with occasional drinkers in the reference group; 297 adjusted. Moderate and heavy RRs, intervals and I² for the mouth and pharynx (72%, 77%), oesophageal SCC (85%, 91%), larynx, colorectum, liver (moderate 1.08, 0.97-1.20) and breast (54%, 10%) match. Heavy-only figures (stomach, pancreas, lung, gallbladder with 8 studies), moderate prostate and melanoma, the inverse figures (kidney, thyroid, Hodgkin's heavy 0.63, non-Hodgkin's heavy 0.75) and the by-design figures (5.34 vs 3.13; 2.79 vs 1.12; 2.81 vs 1.12, with 35/3, 24/7 and 33/3 studies) match. Editors' count for heavy breast: 6 cohort + 5 case-control = 11 (Table 2): same. 50 g/12.5 g = 4 drinks: same. I² up to 91% is the highest in Figure 2 (some area subgroups reach 93%, Table 4). Funding (AIRC project 10258 and FIRC; fellowships from FIRC and Fondazione Umberto Veronesi) and the no-conflict statement match. No quality appraisal is described in the Methods. Publication bias is not examined in this review; the authors refer to their earlier single-site analyses. The Results text describes the melanoma and prostate findings as 'little indication' of an association, whereas the abstract reports an indication of a positive association. The GBD 2016 sentence is not from this source.

anchors.extracted: 572 studies published 1956-2012 with 486,538 cancer cases: 409 (71.5%) case-control, 163 (28.5%) cohort; 541 incidence, 31 mortality; 236 (41.3%) North America, 184 (32.2%) Europe, 101 (17.7%) Asia, 51 (8.9%) other or mixed. 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates, and 138 (24.1%) had occasional drinkers with abstainers in the reference group. The abstract gives heavy-drinking RRs of 5.13, 4.95, 1.44, 2.65 and 1.61 (oral cavity and pharynx, oesophageal SCC, colorectum, larynx, breast), with a clear dose-risk relationship.

Moderate and heavy pooled RRs (random effects) against nondrinkers and occasional drinkers: oral cavity and pharynx 1.83 (1.62-2.07) and 5.13 (4.31-6.10), 52 studies; oesophageal SCC 2.23 (1.87-2.65) and 4.95 (3.86-6.34), 54; breast 1.23 (1.19-1.28) and 1.61 (1.33-1.94), 118; colorectum 1.17 (1.11-1.24) and 1.44 (1.25-1.65), 66; larynx 1.44 (1.25-1.66) and 2.65 (2.19-3.19), 41. Heavy: liver 2.07 (1.66-2.58; 36), stomach 1.21 (1.07-1.36; 39), pancreas 1.19 (1.11-1.28; 39), lung 1.15 (1.02-1.30; 34), gallbladder 2.64 (1.62-4.30; 8). Melanoma moderate 1.20 (1.03-1.41; 14); prostate moderate 1.06 (1.01-1.11) and heavy 1.09 (0.98-1.21; 43); the text calls both 'little indication'. No significant association: oesophageal AC and gastric cardia (25), small intestine (5), cervix (5), endometrium (21), ovary (20), bladder (19), brain (6). Inverse: Hodgkin's heavy 0.63 (0.41-0.97; 9), non-Hodgkin's heavy 0.75 (0.64-0.88; 24), kidney moderate 0.79 (0.72-0.86; 17), thyroid moderate 0.81 (0.71-0.94; 9).

anchors.extracted: Liver moderate 1.08 (0.97-1.20). I² moderate/heavy: oral cavity and pharynx 72%/77%; oesophageal SCC 85%/91% (91% is the highest in the figure); breast 54%/10%; colorectum 52%/69%; liver 45%/79%; larynx 61%/77%. Sites with no clear association at moderate/heavy: oesophageal AC and gastric cardia 0.97 (0.78-1.22)/1.15 (0.95-1.39); small intestine heavy 1.07 (0.67-1.68); bladder heavy 0.95 (0.75-1.20); brain heavy 1.45 (0.69-3.08). Kidney heavy 0.80 (0.57-1.14). Heavy not evaluable for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary, thyroid.

Dose-response meta-regression: risk rises steeply with intake for oral cavity and pharynx and oesophageal SCC, and less steeply for melanoma, colorectum, gallbladder, larynx and breast. Pancreas, lung and prostate show a slight linear increase; stomach and liver risk is raised from about 25 g/day (two drinks). No significant trend for oesophageal AC and gastric cardia, small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain. Lymphoma risk falls with intake; kidney and thyroid are inversely associated at lower doses. Read approximately from the curves at 100 g/day: RR about 8 (oral cavity and pharynx), 7 (oesophageal SCC), 5 (liver), 3.5 (larynx), 2.7 (breast).

anchors.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (men vs women), colorectum rows; Discussion, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Colorectum association stronger in men than women (heterogeneity P = 0.010): men moderate 1.21 (1.11-1.32) and heavy 1.53 (1.30-1.80); women moderate 1.07 (0.99-1.16) and heavy 1.24 (0.68-2.25; 4 studies). No significant colorectal association in women, which the authors note differs from their earlier findings.

anchors.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (by area), melanoma, prostate and non-Hodgkin's rows
anchors.extracted: Melanoma and prostate raised only in North American studies: melanoma light 1.32 (1.11-1.59) and moderate 1.47 (1.14-1.88); prostate 1.05 (1.01-1.09), 1.09 (1.02-1.16) and 1.20 (1.09-1.31) for light, moderate and heavy. Non-Hodgkin's inverse association in Asian and North American but not European studies (P = 0.013).

Restricting to adjusted estimates, and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, did not materially change results (Supplementary S3, not read); the prostate association was clearer in both.

Pancreas: homogeneous across studies. Residual confounding by smoking, overweight and diabetes is a concern, but fully adjusted estimates still gave a significant 20% increase. Prostate is driven by North American studies. Lung (heavy 1.15): residual confounding by smoking may have biased it, and the group's 2011 meta-analysis found no association in never-smokers. Stomach: residual confounding by smoking and by poor diet cannot be ruled out.

Lymphomas: inverse association possibly partly from misclassification, as early symptoms may lead people to quit or reduce drinking; a European cohort of 120,852 people showed no inverse association. Kidney: moderate drinking read as supporting a protective effect on renal cell cancer (8th paragraph), but kidney is listed among cancers with no association in the conclusion (11th). The conclusion states in causal terms that drinking increases risk at the six sites. It says pancreas, prostate and melanoma need more studies, and that the stomach, lung and lymphoma links could be biased by unaccounted confounders and exposure misclassification.

No appraisal of study quality is described in the Methods. Publication bias was not examined in this review; the authors refer to their earlier single-site meta-analyses. Further limitations: high heterogeneity, no pattern or beverage analyses, under-reporting, and possible former drinkers among nondrinkers.
IARC listed alcohol as a carcinogen for the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, liver and larynx in 1988, and added colorectum and female breast in 2010.

key_findings.correction: Add Discussion, 10th paragraph to the locator. The Methods record only whether occasional drinkers were in the reference group; the point about former drinkers comes from the limitations paragraph.

Values and I² match Figure 2. The study counts (52, 54, 41) are site totals. From Table 2 (cohort + case-control), the light estimates rest on 26, 34 and 14 studies, the moderate on 52, 53 and 37, and the heavy on 38, 41 and 36. The larynx light value (0.87) is in Figure 2 only.
Editors' counts recomputed from Table 2: light 42 + 73 = 115, moderate 37 + 58 = 95, heavy 6 + 5 = 11: same. 41 of 118 adjusted (Table 1): same.
The light values for colorectum (0.99) and liver (1.00) are in Figure 2 only.

Worth adding: the between-area heterogeneity tests for these two sites were not significant (P = 0.375 and 0.503, Table 4). Outside the split by area, the light-drinking excess was also significant in men (1.20, 1.06-1.35; 1.39, 1.11-1.74; Table 3) and in case-control studies (1.22, 1.10-1.35; 1.29, 1.07-1.55; Table 2).
Figure 3 viewed: the axis ranges are as stated (0-50 g/day for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary and thyroid).

reporting_issues.note: Heavy-drinking I² values of 73-91% for lung, larynx, oral cavity and pharynx, liver and oesophageal SCC: same.
Stomach row: 33 + 5 = 38 against 39. The design (19 + 20) and area (12 + 8 + 16 + 3) columns sum to 39. Every other row's outcome columns sum to its total.
The same applies to the light-drinking estimates: oral cavity and pharynx light from 26 of 52 studies, oesophageal SCC light from 34 of 54 (Table 2). The light-drinking claim repeats the site totals.
Ovary by design P = 0.007 and lung by area P = 0.045, with heavy drinking 1.26 / 0.96 / 0.92: same.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low confidence; five critical items are clearly not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 15). Item 4 'no' follows the project's rule for an unjustified English-only limit. Item 11 'no' is a close call: the paper states its rule (adjusted when available, otherwise crude) but not a reason. Item 12 'yes' is lenient when no study-level appraisal was done: the adjusted-only and no-occasional-drinker sensitivity analyses address two biases, and their results are only in S3. Neither call changes the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The abstract's Methods also frame the analysis as investigating 'the effect of alcohol', so the causal framing is not confined to the conclusion. Still minor, because for the six named sites it follows IARC's classification, and the Discussion names the main biases.

missed: Light-drinking study counts. The light estimates for the oral cavity and pharynx and for oesophageal SCC rest on 26 and 34 studies (Table 2), not the 52 and 54 printed beside them. This matters for cl_alc_cancer_light, which repeats 52 and 54.

Abstract and Results disagree on melanoma and prostate. The abstract reports an indication of a positive association, while Results, 2nd paragraph says there was 'little indication of an association'.

Categorical and continuous analyses disagree at low intake. The fitted lung curve rises from RR 1 with no dip (Figure 3), although the categorical light RR is 0.84 (0.79-0.88). Oesophageal AC and gastric cardia has a significant light RR (0.86) but no significant dose-response. The low-intake shape is therefore model-dependent.

Light-drinking breast cancer by design (Table 2): cohort 1.06 (1.03-1.10; 42 studies) against case-control 1.04 (0.99-1.09; 73). The light excess is clearer in cohort studies, which bears on the recall-bias argument.

Between-area heterogeneity for the light-drinking oral and oesophageal SCC excess was not significant (P = 0.375, 0.503), so the result being 'significant only in Asian studies' is weaker than a demonstrated regional difference. Discussion, 2nd paragraph offers the ALDH2 variant (28-45% of people in Asian countries) as the explanation.
Replication timeline: 'Heinen et al., a Dutch cohort'. The paper says only 'a European cohort' of 120,852 people; 'Dutch' is not from this source.
